en: Take sure steps upon the ground!
This wretched head of mine—
Do not let a bird of prey devour it,
By falling behind, Taitoru.
Here in this Bukhara,
Oh God, do not let them call me a vagrant woman!
Do not dismiss my words as false;
Do not bring me shame;
Do not bind up my strength;
Do not burn my soul.
Six times, my courser,
I shall look through the spyglass.
If in all six you do not appear, my Bay,
I shall die before my appointed death.
If you fall behind, you wretched horse,
To Almighty God
I entrust you for safekeeping.”
Having spoken these words,
Lamenting, weeping, crying out,
Before the one God, the Creator,
Sobbing still more bitterly,
Her heart painfully torn,
She stood and grew quiet.
Among six hundred and forty-three steeds,
“Into your keeping,” she said of her Bay,
And stood there, having entered him.
Your sister-in-law had entered Taitoru;
To God she repented, again she repented.
Bukhara filled with dust,
And thronged with moving people.
Old Eshen of Bukhara,
With sixty wrestlers beside him,
Was the one driving the horses.
His commander of ten bobbed in the saddle;
Their poles jutted up;
Their wrestlers loomed and flailed;
Their warriors swaggered.
Raising dust along the lower road,
They came out on their way.
As though the horses would not walk,
Striking them once beyond the groin,
They drove them forward with blows.
When your sister-in-law saw old Eshen,
Her anger boiled:
“I feel like seizing this Eshen
And slaughtering him;
I feel like gouging out his eyes.
This Eshen whose way has gone well—
I feel like seizing him along the road,
Dragging him upon the road,
And tearing him apart for the dogs.
If he will not obey when I speak softly,
If he will not move when driven,
This old Eshen here,
Let me seize him on his way
And raise a mighty commotion.
If these men will not obey,
Let me seize them along the road,
Let me gouge out their eyes,
Their sixty or so wrestlers—
Let me slaughter them, sparing not one.”
Having spoken these words,
She shouted in fury.
Your sister-in-law, built like a warrior,
To the sixty wrestlers and Eshen
Called out, “Stand still!
Damn your father’s grave, old Eshen!
My good days are gone; obey me,
Listen to these words of mine.
Sixty wrestlers and old Eshen,
Come, all of you, leaving none behind;
Come, you white-bearded elder!
If you disregard my condition,
If you disobey these words of mine,
You shall see what I have in store for you;
Every last one of you is dead!
Sixty wrestlers and old Eshen,
If you drive the horses, drive them quickly;
Drive every horse hard.
When you drive on from here,
You will pass through Keng-Bulak;
The spur where the mountains end,
You will cross, Eshen, if you live.
Beyond it lies in haze
Broad Bukhara’s great Ak-Chii;
You will pass through great Ak-Chii.
When you pass through mighty Ak-Chii,
There is a ravine with thick-set flanks;
For a rider making the journey,
It is a six-day road.
When you hasten over it,
There is a ridge like a saddle’s back.
Driving onward without sparing the horses,
It is a six-day stretch.
Again, old Eshen, hear my words:
Be sure you make no mistake there.
When you reach that Ak-Chii,
There is no hill the size of a knucklebone,
No hollow the size of a saddlecloth,
No furrow touched by a plow,
No burrow dug by a marmot,
No water for even a tiny sip,
No grass to nibble at;
Gray haze and scorched sand—
Think of this, Eshen:
A wild duck flying there is dazzled;
When a black vulture flies there,
Its wings grow weary on the way.
It stretches to a point in haze,
Its corners shrouded in murk;
You will pass through it if you live.
When you go farther on,
At the spur that slopes inward,
At the overhanging headland,
When you climb onto its back,
My dear Eshen, hear my words:
That is the ridge of It-Torpu.
Across it and down the far side
Lies the desert of It-Olor.
My fine Eshen, hear my words:
Take care there.
Upon the face of the earth, not one twig
Shall I leave, Eshen.
When you go farther on,
Ridge after rugged ridge appears;
A rugged mountain pass appears.
When you go farther on,
Ridge after hilly ridge appears;
A hilly mountain pass appears.
There is no bulging mountain,
No hollow the size of a knucklebone.
Hazy as a saddle’s back,
That is the ridge of Keng-Kepe.
When that plain comes to an end,
Let me tell you what lies beyond:
There is the lake Kara-Dengiz.
If mishap does not trip his feet,
If God does not take the courser,
Let me tell you what it is like:
There is a lake where land disappears.
Drive them all the way there and let them go;
That is the ground for Taitoru.
If you will not heed these words of mine,
To Kara-Dengiz, that great river,
If you will not drive them all the way,
Unable to lower his head to the earth,
Unable to stride like a wild sheep,
If Taitoru falls behind,
Wretched Eshen, if you will not mend your ways,
If you will not follow these words of mine,
If you scorn me because I am a woman,
I shall seize you along the road,
Drag you upon the road,
And tear you apart for the dogs.
I shall gouge out your eyes;
Old Eshen, I shall slaughter you.
The black blood flowing from within you,
I shall scoop up and drink my fill.
Old Eshen, if I do not slaughter you,
If I do not drink my fill of your blood,
My back hair
My very father who begot me,
Temir Khan—may I marry him!
With people calling me a vagrant woman,
How could I remain alive?”
Having said this, Kanykei,
The furious woman, turned and stood.
Hearing this, old Eshen
Was already frightened out of his life;
God had struck Eshen now.
Old Eshen stood thinking;
The haft slipped from his hand;
His heart burst from its casing;
The red blood drained from his face;
Old Eshen’s strength was gone.
His chest began to rattle;
His beard parted strand by strand.
God’s sun in the sky was clouded;
Sixty cares came upon his head at once.
Eshen thought and whimpered;
He pondered, trembling.
His heart was torn with fear;
Kanykei, speaking there,
Seemed like a devouring demon.
He thought and whimpered;
Eshen quivered within.
“If she means to seize us, she will,” he thought.
“This accursed woman,
If Taitoru falls behind,
Leaving not one of us,
Will offer us up as sacrifices,” he thought.
“Leaving none of us at all,
She will wipe us all out,” he thought.
“If she attacks us in the open plain,
From a bitch like this,
Who could beg our lives as a gift?” he thought.
“If her Bay falls behind,
The raging woman will torment us,” he thought.
“If your raging woman attacks,
Who could beg our lives from her?” he thought.
“If she means to destroy us, she will,” he thought.
“This troublemaking bitch
Will raise a commotion,” he thought.
The reason she could do so:
She was a fierce warrior indeed,
Who had thrown the whole world into turmoil;
She was built like a warrior.
When she was the fairest of women,
When this luckless one was a girl,
She grew to maturity like a doe,
Her hair coiled about her head;
She grew to maturity like a deer,
Her hair coiled about her feet;
She stretched gracefully like a tawny doe.
Her speech was sweet, her words were honey;
She became the fairest of women,
A beautiful girl from Bukhara.
Her renown raised dust;
A glowing coal came from the hearth.
Here in this Bukhara,
The fierce woman grew mighty.
Still a playful little child,
She had not yet reached fourteen.
Hero Bakai, the saintly elder,
When the clear-sighted champion saw her,
Disregarding the countless wealth
And livestock he had gathered,
Loaded seventy camels with gold coins
And set out from Kyrgyz Talas.
The beauty among the dark-complexioned,
The radiant one among the Muslims,
He sought then as a bride for Manas.
When the people moved to higher ground,
In the season when horses’ tongues turn dark,
Loading seventy camels with gold coins,
Driving seven thousand barren beasts loose,
When Manas came as the bridegroom
And gave them to her father, Temir Khan,
Her father, Temir Khan,
Gathered treasure and grew rich.
His heart overflowed and was at ease;
Taking the bride-price, Temir Khan
Grew wealthy among the thronging people.
Conceiving a fatal plan,
He gathered the people together.
Out of his joy, Temir Khan
Held eighty feasts by day;
Even the sorrowful rejoiced.
Khan Manas’s ceremonial honors,
In Bukhara with its iron gates,
Were then inscribed upon the door.
Religious masters in motley robes—
When sixty of them were gathered,
Mullahs who read their lessons—
When many had been brought together,
For fierce, bloodthirsty Manas,
